title: Week 79 · Lesson 103: Venous Thromboembolism Management — FNP-Level DVT/PE Recognition, Anticoagulation Safety and Follow-Up

PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 79 — Lesson 103: Venous Thromboembolism Management

FNP-level goal: Recognize possible deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism without relying on one symptom or test, determine when emergency assessment is required, support safe anticoagulation and surveillance after diagnosis, and identify recurrence, bleeding, cancer, pregnancy, and medication-interaction issues that change the care pathway.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain venous thromboembolism using Virchow's triad: stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability.
  • Differentiate DVT and PE symptoms from common mimics while recognizing that clinical appearance alone cannot safely exclude VTE.
  • Use pretest-probability thinking, targeted diagnostic pathways, and emergency disposition rather than indiscriminate D-dimer or imaging orders.
  • Apply anticoagulation safety principles: indication, dose, kidney function, interactions, adherence, bleeding assessment, procedural planning, and pregnancy or cancer context.
  • Recognize post-thrombotic syndrome, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, recurrence, and red flags that require urgent re-evaluation.

Part 1 — VTE Is a Spectrum

Venous thromboembolism includes deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. DVT usually develops in the deep venous system of the legs or pelvis, but it can occur elsewhere. A thrombus can propagate or embolize to the pulmonary circulation, producing PE. The clinical presentation ranges from asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic DVT to hemodynamically unstable PE with shock. The same disease process requires different levels of urgency depending on symptoms, oxygenation, vital signs, and cardiopulmonary reserve.

Virchow's triad structures risk assessment. Stasis can follow immobility, hospitalization, surgery, paralysis, long travel, or heart failure. Endothelial injury can follow trauma, surgery, central venous devices, or inflammation. Hypercoagulability can result from cancer, pregnancy, estrogen exposure, inherited conditions, inflammatory disease, or medication and clinical context. Risk factors improve probability estimation but their absence does not rule out VTE.

Part 2 — DVT: Look Beyond a Swollen Calf

DVT may cause unilateral leg swelling, pain, tenderness, warmth, erythema, superficial venous dilation, or unexplained asymmetry. However, all of these findings can occur with cellulitis, trauma, Baker cyst, muscle strain, lymphedema, chronic venous insufficiency, or superficial thrombophlebitis. Conversely, DVT can have few symptoms. Do not diagnose or exclude DVT from a calf measurement, Homan sign, or visual inspection alone.

Take a focused history: onset and progression, prior VTE, cancer, recent surgery or immobilization, travel, pregnancy or postpartum state, estrogen or testosterone exposure, infection, trauma, smoking, family history, prior thrombophilia tests, current antithrombotics, bleeding risk, and symptoms of PE. Examine both legs, compare circumference when useful, inspect for wounds and cellulitis, palpate tenderness, assess pulses and neurologic function, and look for systemic illness. A cool, pulseless, or neurologically impaired limb follows an arterial emergency pathway, not a routine DVT pathway.

Part 3 — PE: The Dangerous Diagnosis Is Often Nonspecific

PE can present with sudden or unexplained dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, syncope, cough, hemoptysis, hypoxemia, anxiety, or unexplained decline in exercise tolerance. None is sufficiently specific alone. A patient may have normal oxygen saturation and still have PE, especially early or at rest. Conversely, COPD, pneumonia, heart failure, acute coronary syndrome, arrhythmia, anxiety, anemia, pneumothorax, and aortic disease may resemble PE.

Hemodynamic instability changes everything. Hypotension, syncope, severe hypoxemia, severe respiratory distress, altered mental status, signs of shock, or high-risk chest symptoms require emergency transport and resuscitation-capable assessment. In a stable patient with concerning symptoms, use a validated pretest-probability approach and local diagnostic pathway; do not use a D-dimer as a stand-alone rule-out test in high-probability patients or as a substitute for a careful history.

Part 4 — Diagnostics Must Follow Pretest Probability

Pretest probability guides whether testing can begin with D-dimer or should proceed directly to imaging. D-dimer can be useful in selected low- or intermediate-probability patients, but it is nonspecific and may be elevated with age, infection, inflammation, pregnancy, cancer, surgery, or hospitalization. A positive result does not diagnose VTE. Ultrasound is commonly used for suspected lower-extremity DVT; CT pulmonary angiography or ventilation-perfusion imaging may be used for PE depending on the clinical context, contraindications, pregnancy, renal function, contrast allergy, and local access.

The FNP should ask: Is the patient stable? What is the pretest probability? Which test safely answers the question? Is emergency evaluation safer than outpatient testing? Document the rationale and ensure results are tracked. An order that is never completed is not a negative test.

Part 5 — Initial Management Boundaries

Suspected high-risk PE, severe symptoms, instability, active bleeding, pregnancy-related complexity, severe renal dysfunction, or inability to obtain rapid diagnostic testing may require emergency or hospital evaluation. Avoid casually starting, stopping, or changing anticoagulation without a diagnosis and risk assessment unless a protocol and clinician supervision clearly support it. Timing, imaging availability, renal and hepatic function, platelet count, bleeding, and potential procedure needs all matter.

Once VTE is confirmed, anticoagulant selection and duration depend on whether the event was provoked by a transient risk factor, unprovoked, recurrent, cancer-associated, pregnancy-associated, or linked to a persistent risk factor. Direct oral anticoagulants are appropriate in many but not all situations. Pregnancy, mechanical heart valves, antiphospholipid syndrome, severe kidney dysfunction, significant liver disease, drug interactions, extremes of body size, adherence barriers, and cost can alter choices. The FNP supports the shared plan and identifies when hematology, obstetrics, oncology, or anticoagulation specialists are needed.

Part 6 — Anticoagulation Is a System, Not a Prescription Alone

At every anticoagulation visit, verify the drug, dose, indication, start date, intended duration, kidney and liver function when relevant, body weight when dosing requires it, concurrent antiplatelets or NSAIDs, supplements, alcohol use, missed doses, new prescriptions, planned procedures, falls, and bleeding symptoms. Ask specifically about melena, hematemesis, hematuria, heavy vaginal bleeding, persistent epistaxis, severe bruising, dizziness, and head injury.

Educate patients not to double a missed dose unless their drug-specific instructions say to do so, not to share medication, and not to stop treatment before calling the prescriber except in a true emergency pathway. The plan for dental work, colonoscopy, surgery, or pregnancy needs advance coordination. A person receiving anticoagulation who sustains a significant head injury or develops neurologic symptoms requires urgent evaluation even if they initially feel well.

Part 7 — Follow-Up After DVT or PE

Follow-up is not merely confirming that a refill was sent. Review dyspnea, exercise tolerance, chest pain, leg swelling, pain, bleeding, adherence, affordability, compression or activity advice from the treating team, and the duration decision. Clarify whether the event was provoked, what risk factor has resolved or persists, and who will reassess long-term anticoagulation. Do not order routine repeat imaging simply to prove clot disappearance unless a clear clinical question or specialist plan supports it.

Persistent leg discomfort, edema, heaviness, skin changes, or venous ulceration after DVT may represent post-thrombotic syndrome. Persistent or progressive dyspnea, exercise limitation, syncope, or signs of right-heart strain after PE warrant reevaluation for complications such as chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension or another cardiopulmonary diagnosis. Do not label all post-PE breathlessness as deconditioning.

Part 8 — Cancer, Pregnancy, and Estrogen Are Special Contexts

Unprovoked VTE can prompt a careful history, examination, age-appropriate cancer screening review, and individualized discussion; it does not automatically justify indiscriminate whole-body imaging. Active cancer changes recurrence and bleeding risk, drug selection, oncology coordination, and duration decisions. Pregnancy and postpartum status alter both diagnostic and anticoagulant pathways. Patients who are pregnant, recently postpartum, or planning pregnancy require prompt obstetric and hematology-informed coordination.

Review estrogen-containing therapies and other hormonal or medication exposures in context. Do not give universal advice to stop or continue a therapy without understanding why it is used, the timing of the event, pregnancy implications, and alternative options. This is a shared decision with the appropriate prescriber and specialist input.

Part 9 — FNP Case: The Unilateral Swollen Leg

A 56-year-old develops unilateral calf swelling and tenderness after a long hospitalization. The FNP assesses stability, PE symptoms, risk factors, and competing diagnoses; uses a pretest-probability pathway; and arranges timely ultrasound or emergency assessment according to risk and access. A positive D-dimer alone would not establish the diagnosis, and a negative-looking calf would not be enough to dismiss it.

Part 10 — FNP Case: Dyspnea in a Patient on Anticoagulation

A patient taking anticoagulation for prior DVT develops new dyspnea and pleuritic pain after missed doses. The FNP does not assume the medication prevents all recurrence. The patient needs urgent assessment for PE and alternative dangerous diagnoses, medication reconciliation, and a plan that addresses adherence barriers after stabilization.

Part 11 — FNP Case: The Bleeding Call

A patient on a direct oral anticoagulant reports black stool and lightheadedness. The FNP treats this as possible clinically important bleeding, directs urgent evaluation, communicates the drug and timing of last dose, and avoids advising a home dose adjustment as the only response. Anticoagulation benefit must be balanced against active harm in real time.

FNP High-Yield Framework: CLOT

  1. C — Check stability: shock, severe dyspnea, hypoxemia, syncope, active bleeding, or neurologic symptoms demand emergency escalation.
  2. L — Look at probability and mimics: history, examination, risk factors, and competing diagnoses guide testing.
  3. O — Order targeted testing: use validated pathways; D-dimer is neither a diagnosis nor a universal rule-out.
  4. T — Track treatment safely: indication, duration, dose, renal function, interactions, bleeding, procedures, pregnancy, access, and follow-up.

Take-Home Summary

VTE care begins with recognition that DVT and PE are clinical probability problems, not diagnoses made by one sign. Instability and high-risk symptoms require emergency evaluation. After confirmed VTE, safe care means medication-system management, not only a prescription: determine the event context, verify duration and interactions, monitor bleeding and recurrence, and coordinate cancer, pregnancy, hematology, oncology, and procedural issues when indicated.

Educational note: This lesson supports FNP clinical reasoning and does not replace emergency protocols, validated VTE diagnostic pathways, individualized anticoagulation guidance, pregnancy-specific management, or hematology and specialty consultation. New severe dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, hemoptysis, shock, significant bleeding, or acute neurologic symptoms requires emergency evaluation.
